summary: Deprecates the IQUERY operation for inverse DNS lookups from RFC 1035. It was rarely implemented and usually disabled, and pointer records with reverse mapping are the preferred approach. The document tells servers to answer IQUERY requests with a not-implemented error.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS IQUERY tried to find names associated with a record value, but it was rarely used and could be costly for servers. This RFC declares it obsolete and recommends a Not Implemented response.

questions: what is inverse dns lookup iquery
subtitle: Retires the DNS IQUERY operation and updates RFC 1035.

tldr.problem: IQUERY was rarely implemented, often disabled, and could burden servers with expensive searches and very large responses.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC marks opcode 1 obsolete and says name servers SHOULD return a Not Implemented error for IQUERY requests.
tldr.outcome: IQUERY is formally obsolete; the RFC identifies PTR records in the in-addr.arpa tree as the common reverse-mapping approach.

today: RFC 3425 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1035. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What IQUERY Did and Why It Is Retired
sections.content:
IQUERY was a DNS operation for looking up names associated with a supplied resource-record value. The server had to search its database or keep a separate reverse index, which could use significant resources.

The RFC says very large responses could be used in denial-of-service attacks, and operators commonly disabled the operation. It reports no known clients using IQUERY for a meaningful service and points to PTR records in in-addr.arpa as the common reverse mapping method.
sections.plainLanguage: IQUERY asked a server to search for names matching a value. The work and possible response size made it costly, and the RFC says clients did not rely on it.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 1035
sections.content:
This document changes the definition of DNS opcode 1 to identify IQUERY as obsolete. It also supersedes Section 6.4 of RFC 1035, including its subsections.

Name servers SHOULD return a Not Implemented error when they receive an IQUERY request.
sections.plainLanguage: The old IQUERY instructions are no longer in effect. A server should answer an IQUERY request by saying that the operation is not implemented.

sections.title: Security and Opcode Assignment
sections.content:
The RFC says removing IQUERY is unlikely to create new security holes, since the operation was optional and usually disabled. It also notes that securing IQUERY responses with DNSSEC would be difficult without signing them on the fly.

The IQUERY opcode value 1 is permanently retired and must not be assigned to a future opcode.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC retires the unused operation and keeps its number reserved. It notes that supporting and protecting IQUERY responses would also be difficult.
